passage:
Kiran, come and sit. You saw me looking at old photos and asked why my eyes were wet. I'm Baljeet, and I did the same when I was twenty-five: the hostel roof, five of us with paper cups of tea. Rohan was in Dubai, Meena was married in Nagpur, and I was on night shift. I wanted those evenings back.

I didn't demand them. I wrote to Rohan, "Saw the roof photo and laughed for ten minutes. How are you?" He replied within the hour. We planned one video call for Sunday, no big reunion. It wasn't the roof. But it was warm, and it is still going. We speak every couple of months now, and I've stopped waiting for the old days to come round again.

qa.q: Where were Rohan and Meena when Baljeet looked at the photos?
qa.a: Rohan was in Dubai and Meena was married in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling while looking at the old photos?
qa.a: Baljeet felt wistful, eyes wet, wanting those hostel-roof evenings back, but chose not to demand them.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do instead of demanding the old closeness?
qa.a: Baljeet wrote a warm message to Rohan and planned one video call for Sunday, with no big reunion.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt on receiving the message?
qa.a: Rohan replied within the hour, which suggests he was glad to hear from Baljeet.

grounding: An older person recalls scrolling old college photos, missing friends, messaging warmly with a small plan, and accepting that closeness changes shape.

passage:
At one in the morning, in his Gachibowli flat, Tushar was still scrolling. College photos from eight years ago: the hostel roof, Wasim's terrible moustache, the four of them squeezed on one scooter at the lake. He could almost hear Wasim's laugh.

Now Wasim had twins and a job in Pune. They hadn't spoken since his wedding. Tushar felt a slow ache under his ribs. Where had all that closeness gone?

He started typing: "Why don't you ever call?" Then deleted it.

He sent the moustache photo instead. "Found this. Still the worst decision of your life. Miss you, yaar."

In the morning there was a reply. "HAHA burn it. Miss you too. Twins have destroyed me."

Tushar grinned. "I'm in Pune on the 14th for work. Chai for twenty minutes?" "Done."

It wouldn't be the hostel roof. It would be twenty minutes, probably with a baby crying. That was fine.

qa.a: Wasim now had a job in Pune.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he scrolled the old photos?
qa.a: Tushar felt nostalgic and a slow ache of missing Wasim and their old closeness.

qa.q: Why was the message Tushar sent better than the first one he typed?
qa.a: It was warm and light instead of blaming, and it opened the door to a small, realistic plan for chai.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel receiving the photo?
qa.a: Wasim likely felt amused and touched, replying that he missed Tushar too 🙂

grounding: The passage shows a young man who misses a college friend living a different life now, who messages warmly, proposes a small plan and accepts that closeness has changed shape.

passage:
"Rukku? It's Manjula. Is this a bad time?"

"Manju! No, no. I'm just stirring the sambar with a baby on my hip. Talk."

"I was going through the old photos. Remember the rain at Lalbagh, when we missed the last bus?"

"And walked home singing? My mother nearly killed me." Rukmini laughed. "God, I miss that."

"Me too. I miss you. I keep thinking we should go back to how it was. Every weekend together."

A pause. "Manju... I can't do every weekend now. With the baby and Ravi's shifts, I barely see my own face."

Manjula felt a small sting, then let it go. "Okay. What about a call on the first Sunday of every month? Twenty minutes. Sambar optional."

"Yes. That I can do. And when she's older, Lalbagh. In the rain."

"Deal."

Manjula hung up smiling, a little wistful. It wasn't the old friendship. It was still theirs.

qa.q: Where did the friends get caught in the rain?
qa.a: They got caught in the rain at Lalbagh.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel when Rukmini said she couldn't do every weekend?
qa.a: Manjula felt a small sting of disappointment, then let it go and felt wistful but content.

qa.q: How did Manjula adjust her plan, and why did it work?
qa.a: She proposed a monthly twenty-minute call instead of every weekend, which fit Rukmini's life and kept the friendship going.

qa.q: What is the call like for Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini is warm and glad, missing Manjula too, but honest that her life with a baby and a busy partner leaves little time.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young woman who misses an old friend now living a different life, who reaches out warmly, proposes a small plan and accepts that closeness changes shape.
